newsitem.title: USA: Brooke says pact would bankrupt Liggett.
newsitem.headline: Brooke says pact would bankrupt Liggett.

text.p: Brooke Group Ltd on Monday lashed out against the landmark tobacco settlement, saying the accord would bankrupt its Liggett cigarette unit and does not include protections that had been set under its own settlement reached in March.

Attorney Marc Kasowitz, who represents Brooke and negotiated its March tobacco settlement, told Reuters that the deal struck on Friday unfairly burdens Liggett, maker of Chesterfield and Lark cigarettes.

"You really have an unfair, ironic and outrageous situation here. The one company that had the courage and took the steps of breaking with the entire industry...is now in a posiition where it's going to be bankrupt if the settlement is enacted into legislation," he said in a telephone interviiew.

Brooke Group, run by controversial businessman Bennett LeBow, stunned the tobacco industry by settling litigation with states that had sued the industry. In return for immunity from lawsuits, Liggett agreed to pay states 25 percent of its pretax profits for the next 25 years into a settlement fund.

Under the March settlement, attorneys general and tobacco plaintiffs agreed to use their "best efforts" to ensure that Brooke and Liggett's liability under a global legislative settlement would not be more onerous than the existing terms.
But Kasowitz said the deal announced on Friday did not provide any provisions to ensure that Liggett would be limited to terms set out in the March agreement.

"We were under the impression that Liggett was going to be protected according to the contract that we had with the attorneys general. We were being told that...right up until the eve of the signing of the agreement," he said.

Tobacco companies agreed Friday to pay a staggering $368.5 billion to settle a flood of lawsuits that have gripped the powerful industry. In return, the deal calls for the companies to be granted immunity from any lawsuits for actions that might have taken place in the past.

"What that settlement purports to do is to impose payment obligations on Liggett on top of the obligations it already has and the payment of those obligations would mean bankruptcy for Liggett," said Kasowitz of law firm Kasowitz, Benson, Torres & Friedman.
He also expressed concern that internal industry documents would not be disclosed under the deal. As part of its settlement, Liggett agreed to turn over internal documents.
"If there's going to be some kind of global deal, there ought to be a full accounting," Kasowitz said.
The settlement is widely expected to undergo intense scrutiny in Washington, where politicians already are vowing to make major revisions.

"We think when these facts are appropriately brought to light in the various places, in Congress and every place else, that the right action will be taken with respect to this legislation. Obviously, we're just at the beginning," Kasowitz said.
